16. Let us first consider the scope of Section 157(2) and whether the Legislature‘s use of only the term ―removal‖ in the said section, while excluding the other verbs used in clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) (i.e. carrying, depositing, harbouring, keeping, concealing etc.) from the provision specifying the scope of confiscation, was intentional and requires restrictive interpretation of the word ―remove‖.

The cardinal principle: penal and fiscal statutes must be strictly construed 17. The principles of statutory interpretation are fairly settled. A Court must give meaning and effect to the words used by the legislature in a statute in order to garner legislative intent (see for example Federation of Pakistan vs. Durrani Ceramics (2014 PTD 2016), Jamat-I-Islami vs. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2000 SC 111) and Standard Printing Press vs. Sind Employee’s Social Security Institution (1988 SCMR 91). A Court cannot read into the statue in view of the established doctrine of casus omissus (see for example Gul Taiz Khan 23 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 Marwat vs. Registrar, Peshawar High Court (PLD 2021 SC 391). A Court is also not to give meaning to the language of a provision in such manner that it renders the provision redundant.

18. A settled principle of statutory interpretation is that provisions of penal statutes are to be construed strictly and in case multiple interpretations are possible, the construction most beneficial to an accused is to be preferred. It was held by the Supreme Court in Muhammad Ali vs. The State Bank of Pakistan (1973 SCMR 140) that, “we are dealing here with a penal statute, the provisions of which must be interpreted strictly, and in case of any ambiguity or doubt arising from the construction, the benefit must go to the accused person”. This principle was reiterated in The Collector of Customs vs. Messrs. Abdul Majid Khan (1977 SCMR 371) and more recently in Tahir Naqash vs. The State (PLD 2022 SC 385) wherein it was reemphasized that, “the rule of interpretation has been evolved according to which a penal statute should be strictly construed in favour of the accused.” (Also see State Bank Of Pakistan Vs Securities and Exchange Commission Of Pakistan (PLD 2018 Supreme Court 52), Zahid Rehman vs The State (PLD 2015 SC 77), Chairman Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Bahawalpur vs. Rizwan Rasheed (2005 SCMR 728), Province of Punjab vs. Muhammad Rafiq (PLD 2018 SC 178), Brig. (Retd.) F.B. ALI vs The State (PLD 1975 SC 506)).

19. In Telenor Pakistan (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (I.T.R. No.63 of 2015) the settled principles guiding the interpretation of a fiscal statute were summarized, in view of the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Federation of 24 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 Pakistan through Secretary Ministry of Finance and others v. Haji Muhammad Sadiq and others (PLD 2007 SC 133), Aslam Industries Ltd., Khanpur v. Pakistan Edible Corporation of Pakistan and others (1993 SCMR 683) Collector of Customs (Appraisement), Karachi and others v. Messrs Abdul Majeed Khan and others (1977 SCMR 371) and Messrs Hirjina & Co. (Pakistan) Ltd., Karachi v. Commissioner of Sales Tax Central Karachi (1971 SCMR 128), as follows:

―If a provision of a taxing statute can have two reasonable explanations, then one which is favorable to the taxpayer has to be accepted and any ambiguity is required to be resolved in favour of the tax payer. Likewise, redundancy cannot be attributed to the lawmaker. Every word and part of the statute has to be given meaning and effect. It is always presumed that the legislature has used every word in a context and for a purpose. The statute has to be read as a whole and the intention of the legislature has to be discovered by paying attention to what has been said. It is settled law that while interpreting fiscal statutes the Court looks at what is clearly said. There is no room for any intendment, there is no equity about a tax, nothing is to be read in or implied and one must only look fairly at the language used.‖ The principle of Expressio Unius Est Exclusio Alterius 20. The maxim expressio unius est exclusio alterius (the express mention of one thing excludes others) is a well-established canon of statutory interpretation. This principle is attracted where the Legislature uses a series of words or terms in one provision but omits certain words or terms from another or related provision within the same statute.

21. In our present context, the Legislature has used seven distinct verbs in Clause (89) of Section 156(1) to describe the 25 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 various ways a person can be concerned with smuggled goods i.e. carrying, removing, depositing, harbouring, keeping, concealing, and dealing. But in Section 157(2), which authorizes the confiscation of vehicles, the Legislature used only one of these verbs —"remove‖— while choosing not to include the others. Such choice of text cannot be deemed accidental. If the Legislature had intended that any vehicle used for ‗carrying‘ or ‗transporting‘ proscribed goods should be confiscated, it could easily have said so. It did not. The principle of expressio unius therefore dictates that the power to confiscate vehicles under Section 157(2) must be read as being limited to vehicles used for ―removal‖ of proscribed goods, without expanding the scope of the penal provision by reading into it, for purposes of confiscation, vehicles carrying or transporting smuggled goods.

Harmonious Construction: Giving meaning to all words 22. The principle of noscitur a sociis signifies that a word is known by the company it keeps. The Legislature often uses synonymous words in a statutory provision to cover a broad range of acts. It does so in Clause (89) of Section 156(1) for example, where ―removing‖ appears alongside ―carrying, depositing, harbouring, keeping or concealing.‖ In the context of smuggling or indulging in the import of prohibited goods, the words cover a range of actions that form part of such felonious trade. But each of these words has a distinct meaning. Having used such words together as part of Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1), the use of the words ―removal‖ alone in Section 157(2) of the Act is not without significance.

23. As noted above, a fundamental rule of statutory interpretation is that the Court must give meaning to every word 26 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 used by the Legislature and must not render any part of the statutory text redundant. Sections 2(s), 156 and 157 of the Customs Act, which are penal provisions within a fiscal statute, are to be construed according to the fair commonsense meaning of the language used. It would not be without doing serious violence to the English language for one to conclude that the Legislature employed the word ―remove‖ when it meant ―carry‖ or ―transport‖. When we deliver a package to a courier company or book freight on a truck, we don‘t say ―can you please have this removed to such and such location?‖ We use the words ‗carry‘ or ‗transport‘ or ‗send‘ to describe the act of conveyance of goods from one place to another, in accordance with the ordinary meaning of such words.

24. If ―removal‖ in Section 157(2) were interpreted to mean ―carrying‖, the Legislature's use of a different word in the provision would be rendered meaningless. Similarly, if ―removal‖ were interpreted to encompass all the verbs in Clause (89) of Section 156(1) of the Customs Act, the Legislature's specific enumeration of seven distinct acts would be rendered superfluous. The distinction between ―carrying‖ and ―removing‖ is not merely semantic but reflects a substantive textual and legal difference. ―Carrying‖ typically refers to the physical act of transporting goods from one place to another. It is a neutral term that describes the means by which goods move. A vehicle used for carrying goods is simply the instrument of transportation. ―Removal‖, on the other hand, carries a more specific connotation. Thus, while ―carrying‖ focuses on the physical act of transportation, the word ―removal‖ has been repeatedly used within the Act to refer to the action of taking goods out of custody or control within a customs area or warehouse etc.

27 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 The Legislative intent reflecting a rational policy choice 25. The Legislature's decision to limit confiscation to vehicles used for ―removal‖ of proscribed goods rather than those carrying or transporting such goods appears to be a rational policy choice. It reflects the adoption of the principle of proportionality while applying a penal sanction. Confiscation of a vehicle is a severe penalty. The principle of proportionality requires that the punishment fit the gravity of the offence. The Legislature may have determined that confiscation is an appropriate penalty only where the vehicle is used for the proximate act of removing goods from a border/border post or a warehouse as part of the final act that consummates the offence of smuggling, rather than for mere transportation of goods where such act is removed from the offense of smuggling and the transporter may have no means to determine, even while exercising diligence, that the goods in question are smuggled or otherwise proscribed. Further, the object of the Act is to prevent, deter and punish smuggling or import/export of proscribed goods. By limiting confiscation to vehicles used for ―removal‖ of smuggled or prohibited or non-duty paid goods, the Legislature may have intended to penalize those most directly involved with and thus aiding and abetting the smuggling operation.

26. The words used in Clause (89) of Section 156(1) of the Act can be arranged along a spectrum of culpability. ―Removing‖ suggests a proximate act to taking goods from the border/entry point into the country and/or a greater degree of participation in an act of taking goods from lawful control, while ―carrying‖ may involve a lesser degree of participation in taking goods from the entry point into the country or from lawful control. It appears that 28 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 the Legislature intended to expand the scope of the confiscatory penalty for the more culpable form of participation in smuggling or import/export of otherwise proscribed goods. This hierarchical approach to penalties is evident in the structure of Section 156 of the Act as a general matter, which prescribes different penalties for different offences, while reserving harsher punishments for the more odious acts.

27. Examples from other jurisdictions also suggest that the word ―removal‖ is accorded a distinct legal meaning. The term ―removal‖ in customs legislation across common law jurisdictions has historically carried a specific technical meaning: the act of taking goods out of customs control or custody, particularly at the point of entry or exit. For example, in United States v. Harold (588 F.2d 1136 (5th Cir. 1979)), the US Court of Appeals held that, ―removal of goods from Customs custody or control is the movement of property in Customs custody or control with felonious intent. Any appreciable change of the location of the property with felonious intent, whether there is actual removal of it from the owner's premises or not, constitutes the removal element of the offense.‖ The Legislative scheme: border-related versus inland enforcement 28. The scheme of the Act suggests that the Legislature drew a distinction between conveyances used in the actual act of smuggling across the border and the proximate act of removing such goods from the border or a customs post/warehouse on the one hand, and those used for inland transportation of smuggled/proscribed goods on the other. If the Legislature intended to confiscate any vehicle that carried, at any time, 29 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 smuggled or proscribed goods within the country, it would have used broader language such as ―used for the carrying, transporting, or conveying‖ of such goods. It did not.

29. The definition of ―smuggling‖ in Section 2(s) focuses on the act of bringing goods into or taking them out of Pakistan ―by any route other than a route declared under section 9 or section 10” or “bringing into Pakistan or taking out of Pakistan…by any such route, any goods which are dutiable or prohibited goods and evading payment of duties or taxes or contravening any prohibition or restriction…” As is evident, what is proscribed is the cross-border act of bringing goods illegally into Pakistan or taking them out. The inland possession of smuggled goods does not constitute ―smuggling‖, but constitutes a separate offence of, inter alia, ―possession‖ under clause (89) of Section 156(1) of the Act.

30. Section 157(2) provides for confiscation of “every conveyance of whatever kind used in the removal of any goods liable to confiscation under this Act”. The phrase ―used in the removal‖ is in the past tense and suggests a completed act of removal that is directly connected to the commission of the offence of smuggling or the offence of importing or exporting prohibited or non-duty paid goods. The ordinary textual reading of Section 157(2) is that it refers to a conveyance that is instrumental in the act of removing goods (i) brought in from an undeclared route on the border, or (ii) from customs control at a declared route or a warehouse, which goods are smuggled/prohibited or in relation to which duties and taxes have not been paid, thus making the conveyance being proximately connected to the act of smuggling or importing/exporting prohibited or non-paid goods.

30 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 31. If ―removal‖ in Section 157(2) is expansively read to include inland carriage, a transporter who innocently carries goods (without the knowledge that they are smuggled or proscribed) would end up having his vehicle confiscated, which is the same penalty that applies to a smuggler or an aider/abettor using his/her vehicle to bring such goods across the border or removing them from the border. Such outcome would violate the principle of proportionality and disregard the hierarchy of culpability that flows out of the scheme of Section 156 of the Act. A vehicle proximately involved in the removal of goods liable for confiscation is the instrument of the principal offence and may justly be forfeited. A vehicle used for inland carriage of goods liable to confiscation is several steps removed from the act of smuggling or import/export of prohibited and/or non-duty paid goods liable to confiscation, and ought not be subject to the harsh penalty of confiscation prescribed for the act of smuggling, or any penalty at all, to the extent that the owner can establish lack of knowledge regarding their proscribed character and/or another legitimate excuse for carriage of such goods.

Implications for the Interpretation of S.R.O. 499(I)/2009 32. The interpretation of ―remove‖ in Section 157(2) has direct implications for the application of S.R.O. 499 and S.R.O. 1619. Those SROs mandate confiscation of "lawfully registered conveyance including packages and containers... found carrying smuggled goods". The scope of confiscation, extending to conveyances, is prescribed by Section 157(2) of the Act, which speaks only of vehicles used ―for the removal‖ of goods liable to confiscation. By extending the sanction of confiscation of vehicles, used for ―carrying smuggled goods‖, the SROs exceed the scope of 31 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 confiscation authorized by the parent statute. It should require no elaboration that SROs issued under Section 181 cannot override or modify the parent law and must operate within the four corners of the Act and in consonance with the objects of the Act.

33. Thus, while S.R.O. 499 and 1619 may validly remove the option to pay a fine in lieu of confiscation for certain classes of goods, they cannot expand the category of conveyances subject to confiscation beyond what Section 157(2) authorizes. If a vehicle is purportedly used for inland transportation or carrying of goods liable to confiscation, but not for ―removal‖ of smuggled or proscribed goods as explained above, such vehicle is not liable for confiscation in terms of Section 157(2) the Act. It does not fall within the province of the FBR to create a penal sanction by executive diktat when the law doesn‘t provide for it.

34. The Legislature deliberately chose not to include ―carrying‖, ―depositing‖, ―harbouring‖, ―keeping‖, ―concealing‖ or ―transporting‖ in Section 157(2) of the Act, while prescribing confiscation for vehicles ―removing‖ goods liable to confiscation. Applying the principle of expressio unius est exclusio alterius, this omission is intentional and must be given effect. The power to confiscate vehicles under Section 157(2) is limited to vehicles used for the removal of smuggled or otherwise prescribed goods, not those merely transporting or carrying such goods, where the act of transporting or carrying is not proximate to the act of smuggling or carrying proscribed goods across the border, and does not qualify as partaking in ―removal‖ of such goods.

35. This restrictive interpretation is reinforced by the principles of strict construction applicable to penal and fiscal statutes, the requirement of proportionality applicable to the punishment of 32 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 confiscation, and the need to give meaning to every word used by the Legislature in defining the scope of the offences in clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) read with Section 157(2), which defines the scope of confiscation applicable to conveyances in relation to such offences. While S.R.O. 499 and 1619 effectively remove the discretion to levy a fine in lieu of confiscation, they cannot expand the statutory basis for confiscation itself, which remains confined to vehicles used for ―removal‖ of smuggled/proscribed goods in terms of Section 157(2) of the Act.

Offences in Clause (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) and the requirement of mens rea 36. Two central questions that arise in relation to the interpretation of the SROs 499 and 1619 are: (i) whether the offence of possessing, carrying, or dealing with smuggled goods, or prohibited, or non-duty paid goods, as the case may be, under Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Act is an offence of strict liability; and (ii) whether the extent of confiscation prescribed in terms of Section 157(2) of the Act constitutes an element of the offences prescribed under Section 156(1) of the Act. The Customs Department appears to have understood the said SROs as having mandated confiscation of vehicles found carrying or transporting smuggled goods within Pakistan, irrespective of the vehicle owner's knowledge or culpability re the proscribed nature of such goods. This Court must first determine whether such an interpretation aligns with the foundational principles of penal liability as settled in our jurisprudence, within the context of the scheme prescribed by the Legislature in terms of Sections 2(s), 156, 157, 181 and 187 of the Act.

37. The principle of individual responsibility is the cornerstone of our penal system. Deterrence, as an object of penal law, relies on 33 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 individual autonomy. Sanctions and penalties are a legitimate means to establish deterrence when they serve to reduce or prevent harm knowingly brought about or risked by an individual. That makes, as a general rule, culpability a precondition for imposition of penalty. As was held in Haji Abdul Razzak v. Pakistan (PLD 1974 SC 5): “there must be some culpability or negligence in the person sought to be made liable”. In view of the principles of reasonability and proportionality, in terms of applying sanctions, it appears grossly unjust to confiscate property of a wholly innocent person used without their consent, connivance, or knowledge. Any penal scheme established by law ordinarily requires the attribution of wrongdoing (which can take the form of an act or omission) to an individual before a penalty can be imposed on them, with strict liability offenses being a narrow exception.

38. Professor Andrew Ashworth in Principles of Criminal Law (3rd Edition, Oxford University Press, 1999) contends that the principle of legality can be divided into three distinct principles: the principle of retroactivity; the principle of maximum certainty; and the principle of strict construction of penal statutes. The principle of fair warning is treated as a subset of the principle of certainty in a sense that a rational, autonomous individual with a moral compass ought to have no undue difficulty in ascertaining the law when forewarned. Professor Ashworth argues that, “an individual should only be held criminally liable for consequences that were knowingly brought about or knowingly risked … the essence of the principle of autonomy is that the incidence and degree of criminal liability should respect the choices made by the individual. The principle of mens rea expresses this by stating that defendants should only be 34 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 held criminally liable for events or consequences which they intended or knowingly risked.”

39. That a person should be presumed innocent until proven guilty as a principle of procedural fairness is as old as the hills. It is well understood that placing a presumption of guilt upon an accused would amount to an oppressive burden on individual citizens and would vest immense power in the hands of state officials, which would be liable to abuse. It is thus that even where the onus of proof is placed on the shoulders of a defendant, it is treated as a preliminary burden that stands discharged where the defendant can make out a prima facie case in his defence, and the burden then shifts back to the prosecution. Likewise, as an interpretive tool, the principle of strict construction requires that any doubt in the meaning of a statutory provision be resolved in favour of the defendant. This principle guides the interpretive exercise undertaken by the Courts such that any doubt about the legislative purpose is to be resolved in favour of the defendant.

40. The principles governing the requirement of wrongdoing and culpability have been enumerated in detail by this Court in Lal Mat Khan where the Court undertook a holistic appraisal of the Customs Act in light of constitutional guarantees, particularly Articles 9, 10A, 23, and 24 of the Constitution. In Lal Mat Khan this Court re-emphasized the following fundamental principles, which are pivotal to the matter at hand:

(a) Principle of Individual Autonomy: The Court invoked HLA Hart's philosophy, noting that penal systems are founded on individual responsibility. “A person must not be punished if no wrongdoing can be attributed to him/her”. To argue otherwise would be to claim that our Constitution 35 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 permits punishment without culpability (see paras 59 and 60).

(b) Culpability as a Prerequisite: In Haji Abdul Razzak v. Pakistan (PLD 1974 SC 5), the Supreme Court held that the “accepted principle for the imposition of a penalty is that there must be some culpability or negligence in the person sought to be made liable.” It was further observed that “no innocent person should be unjustly punished or deprived of his property” A finding of fault, or at least a failure to establish a lawful excuse, is thus a necessary precondition to a penal sanction, including confiscation of property.

(c) Confiscation as a Penalty: The Court held that confiscation of property, even though in rem proceedings under the Act, constitutes a penalty. It cannot be disguised as a mere administrative action against the property itself without impacting the owner's constitutional right to property. The Court noted that “merely because there is no stigma attached to the person of the owner of the property being confiscated does not mean that civil forfeiture/confiscation of property is not a penalty” (see para. 191).

The principle against strict liability 41. Strict liability is a term used to identify offences for which a person may be held liable without proof of intention, knowledge, recklessness or negligence. The rationale for strict liability, as explained in academic literature, is that it is aimed at social protection in cases where it is not feasible to establish intent (in minor regulatory offences for example) or where the harm inflicted is so significant that punishment must follow (in cases such as manslaughter for example). Other than administrative policy, another argument made in favour of strict liability is that in cases of trivial offences (for example speeding etc.) conducting a 36 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 complete trial to establish intent is not worth the public expenditure involved in prosecution and paying for Court time.

42. The law across common law jurisdictions maintains a strong presumption that mens rea (a guilty mind) is required for every offence unless the legislature explicitly states otherwise. In Morissette v. United States (342 U.S. 246), the US Supreme Court held that the “mere omission from a statute of any mention of intent” should not be construed as eliminating the intent requirement. Strict liability is generally reserved for ―public welfare offenses‖ with light penalties, not those involving property forfeiture.

43. In Brend v. Wood ((1946) 175 L.T. 306), Lord Goddard C.J. observed that, ―it is of the utmost importance for the protection of the liberty of the subject that a court should always bear in mind that, unless a statute, either clearly or by necessary implication, rules out mens rea as a constituent part of a crime, the court should not find a man guilty of an offence against the criminal law unless he has a guilty mind.‖ In Lim Chin Aik v. The Queen ([1963] A.C. 160), the Privy Council declared that, ―proof of the existence of a guilty intent is an essential ingredient of a crime at common law is not at all in doubt.‖ 44. Sweet v. Parsley ([1970] AC 132) is a seminal English case where considerations in determining whether an offense can be construed as one of strict liability were detailed. It will be useful for our purposes to reproduce the judgment at some length. The relevant facts were that Stephanie Sweet, the sub-tenant of a farmhouse, let out several rooms to tenants. While she wasn‘t personally living there, she visited occasionally to collect letters and rent. Drugs, including cannabis resin, were found in the 37 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 farmhouse and Ms. Sweet was charged with being concerned in the management of premises used for the purpose of smoking cannabis resin, contrary to section 5(b) of the Dangerous Drugs Act, 1965. The appellant conceded that the premises had been so used, and the prosecution acknowledged that she did not know this. She was convicted of the offence, which conviction was set aside by the House of Lords. Lord Reid noted that:

“Sometimes the words of the section which create a particular offence make it clear that mens rea is required in one form or another. Such cases are quite frequent. But in a very large number of cases there is no clear indication either way. In such cases there has for centuries been a presumption that Parliament did not intend to make criminals of persons who were in no way blameworthy in what they did. That means that whenever a section is silent as to mens rea there is a presumption that, in order to give effect to the will of Parliament, we must read in words appropriate to require mens rea… mens rea is an essential ingredient of every offence unless some reason can be found for holding that that is not necessary…”

45. Lord Pearce articulated the exception to the rule, while qualifying it, by noting that, “those who undertake various industrial and other activities, especially where these affect the life and health of the citizen, may find themselves liable to statutory punishment regardless of knowledge or intent, both in respect of their own acts or neglect and those of their servants. But one must remember that normally mens rea is still an ingredient of any offence…It is one thing to make a man absolutely responsible for all his own acts and even vicariously liable for his servants if he engages in a certain type of activity. But it is quite another matter to make him liable for persons over whom he has no control.”

46. The opinion of Lord Diplock is also helpful in explaining the rationale for strict liability: “Where penal provisions are of general 38 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 application to the conduct of ordinary citizens in the course of their everyday life the presumption is that the standard of care required of them in informing themselves of facts which would make their conduct unlawful, is that of the familiar common law duty of care. But where the subject-matter of a statute is the regulation of a particular activity involving potential danger to public health, safety or morals in which citizens have a choice as to whether they participate or not, the court may feel driven to infer an intention of Parliament to impose by penal sanctions a higher duty of care on those who choose to participate and to place upon them an obligation to take whatever measures may be necessary to prevent the prohibited act, without regard to those considerations of cost or business practicability which play a part in the determination of what would be required of them in order to fulfil the ordinary common law duty of care. But such an inference is not lightly to be drawn, nor is there any room for it unless there is something that the person on whom the obligation is imposed can do directly or indirectly, by supervision or inspection, by improvement of his business methods or by exhorting those whom he may be expected to influence or control, which will promote the observance of the obligation.”

47. In Gammon v. Attorney General for Hong Kong [1985 AC1] the Privy Council, while holding the statutory provision in question before it attracted strict liability, summarized the relevant principles and formulations of law as follow:
(1) there is a presumption of law that mens rea is required before a person can be held guilty of a criminal offense;
(2) the presumption is particularly strong where the offense is truly criminal in character;
39 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 (3) the presumption applies to statutory offences, and can be displaced only if this is clearly or by necessary implication the effect of the statute;

(4) the only situation in which the presumption can be displaced is where the statute is concerned with an issue of social concern. Public safety is such an issue. (5) even where a statute is concerned with such an issue, the presumption of mens rea stands unless it can also be shown that the creation of strict liability will be effective to promote the objects of the statute by encouraging greater vigilance to prevent the commission of the prohibited act.

Professor Ashworth argues in Principles of Criminal Law (pp.175) that, “strict liability should not be imposed where there is nothing more a defendant could reasonably be expected to do in order to avoid the harm.”

48. The Indian Supreme Court in State of Maharashtra v. Mayer Hans George (AIR 1965 SC 722) noted that while certain regulatory statutes may attract strict liability, the presumption of mens rea remains unless the ―object of the statute‖ would be defeated without it. This case involved a German national smuggling gold into India. The Indian Supreme Court noted that ignorance of law was no excuse, and further that the need to establish mens rea would defeat the objects of the statute enacted to curb financial crimes. In Nathulal v. State of M.P. (AIR 1966 SC 43), the Indian Supreme Court held that for a statutory offence, the requirement of mens rea is to be read into the statute unless it is expressly excluded. While interpreting provisions of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, the court held that the object of the statute was public welfare and regulation of trade, not to punish innocent individuals burdened by negligence. And that 40 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 imposition of severe penalties without establishing intent would contravene justice and fairness.

49. Clause (89) of Section 156(1) seeks to penalize a person who is ―in possession of, or is in any way concerned in carrying... smuggled goods... without lawful excuse, the proof of which shall be on such person.‖ The inclusion of the phrase ―without lawful excuse‖ relates to the mental element. While Section 156, read with Section 187 of the Act, places the initial burden of proof on the accused, this does not transform the offence into a strict liability one. The scheme of discharge of onus of proof merely reflects that the facts relating to any ―lawful excuse‖ (such as a bona fide purchase or lack of knowledge etc.) would ordinarily be within the peculiar knowledge of the possessor. In Lal Mat Khan, the Court emphasized the shifting nature of the burden of proof, borrowing from Kamran Industries v. Collector of Customs (PTCL 1996 CL 15) and Abdul Razzaq v. Directorate General of Intelligence (2016 PTD 1861). The accused's initial burden is an ―evidential and tactical burden‖ to establish a prima facie case of lawful excuse. The legal burden to prove that the goods are smuggled and that the person concerned has no lawful excuse remains ultimately with the prosecution/Customs Department. The Customs Department cannot rely on the mere existence of smuggled goods in a conveyance undertaking an inland journey to automatically impose the penalty of confiscation on the vehicle, without establishing some nexus of culpability or knowledge (actual or constructive) on the part of the owner of the conveyance.

50. In a just penal system, punishment cannot lie wherever it falls. A system that punishes the unlucky as opposed to the guilty 41 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 would lose its moral authority and fail to act as a mechanism for social control and public welfare. The ordinary presumption that a person cannot be held liable for an offense without a finding of wrongdoing on his/her part can only be rebutted by express words used by the legislature or by necessary implication, in order to protect the innocent from punishment, ensure that the state proves moral blameworthiness, and uphold the rule of law. In Lal Mat Khan it was noted that “the State cannot employ provisions of the Customs Act as a weapon to trap innocent owners of property, and commandeer or forfeit such assets for its own use without payment of compensation" (see para. 191).

51. In our present context, the definition of offences under subclauses (8), (9), (89), (90) of Section 156(1), read with section 2(s) of the Act, do not support the proposition that the said offences were designed by the legislature as attracting strict liability. The object of the Customs Act is to prevent smuggling and the import/export of prohibited goods, and the import of goods without payment of duties and taxes. Section 2(s) includes within the definition of smuggling “an attempt, abetment or connivance” to bring in or take out from Pakistan smuggled goods. Clause (8) of section 156(1) defines the act of smuggling goods into or out of Pakistan as an offence. Clause (9) of section 156 (1) deals with the offence of importing into or exporting from Pakistan goods by evading payment of duties or importing or exporting prohibited goods. Clause (89) of section 156(1) defines the acquisition, possession, carrying, removing, depositing, harbouring, keeping or concealing smuggled goods without lawful as an offence. It includes within such offence, the act of dealing with smuggled goods, “where there may be reasonable suspicion that they are 42 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 smuggled goods”. Clause (90) of section 156(1) defines the act of acquisition, possession, carrying, removing, depositing, harbouring, keeping or concealing proscribed goods other than smuggled goods as an offence. Clauses (89) and (90) also explicitly provide for lawful excuse on part of the accused as a defence.

52. The text of clauses (89) and (90) of section 156(1) therefore clearly establishes that the legislature intended mens rea to be established in relation to both offences. The Legislature provided, in relation to the offence defined under clause (89), that mens rea in dealing with smuggled goods may include recklessness for purposes of establishing liability, to the extent that an ordinary prudent person would nurture reasonable suspicion that the goods may be smuggled. In other words, for purposes of clause (89) of section 156(1) reckless disregard of the possibility that the goods in question may be smuggled would suffice for establishment of liability. It is well understood that in offences related to possession, knowledge becomes the key element in the crime. Thus, where a reasonable person ought to be aware that there is a risk that the goods in question may be smuggled but the person goes ahead and takes the risks of dealing in such goods, such wilful blindness constitutes the failure to discharge the duty to inquire and would satisfy the requirement of wrongdoing. In such circumstances, the adjudicatory authority can infer ‗knowledge‘ from exhibition of wilful blindness to the suspicion that ought to inform a prudent person.

53. In West Minister City Council v. Croyalgrange Ltd. [1986] 83 Cr. App. R155 the House of Lords held that, “it is always open to a tribunal of fact, when knowledge on part of a defendant is required to be proved, to base a finding of knowledge 43 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 on evidence that the defendant had deliberately shut his eyes to the obvious or refrained from inquiry because he suspected that truth but did not want to have his suspicion confirmed.” The same principle would also apply when it comes to the establishment of recklessness in relation to reasonable suspicion for purposes of clause (89) of section 156(1) of the Act. Therefore, to read Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) as offences of strict liability, where the mere actus reus of transporting smuggled goods automatically results in the mandatory confiscation of the vehicle without any requirement to prove the owner's knowledge, connivance, or recklessness toward his duty of care, would fly in the face of this well-settled jurisprudential foundation. Such interpretation would render the phrase ―without lawful excuse‖ otiose and would violate the constitutional guarantees of due process, liberty and property rights under Articles 9, 10A, 23 and 24 of the Constitution. The offences defined by clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Act are not strict liability offences and require the establishment of wrongdoing on part of a defendant, which can stand established where a defendant fails to establish a lawful excuse for possession of smuggled or prohibited or non-duty paid goods.

The scope of Section 181: defining punishment, not the offense 54. A critical legal error that appears to have marred the approach of the Customs Department to implementing provisions of the Act is its sense that legal instruments issued in exercise of delegated authority under section 181 of the Act can override or supplant the definition of offences and their constituent elements as prescribed under section 156 of the Act. Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) specifically include the phrase ―without lawful excuse, the proof of which shall be on such person‖. This explicitly 44 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 builds a fault-based defence into the definition of the offence. Section 181 vests the FBR with the power to determine where a ―fine in lieu of confiscation‖ is prohibited. The adjudicatory scheme prescribes a common-sensical sequence.

55. The first order of business for an adjudicator is to determine whether the constituent elements of the offence under the relevant clause of Section 156(1) are made out. Only after an offence is made out can one move on, as step two, to the second column of the table under Section 156(1) of the Act, to consider the question of punishment. And it is in considering the nature of punishment to be meted out that Section 181 of the Act becomes relevant, as it confers authority on the FBR to oust any discretion vested in the adjudicatory authorities to impose redemption fine in lieu of the harsher punishment of confiscation, in the event that such punishment is prescribed by Section 156(1) of the Act. To state the obvious, FBR cannot use its power under Section 181 to strip away the ―lawful excuse‖ requirement of Section 156 or to prescribe the punishment of confiscation of goods (including vehicles) where the same is not provided by the Act. SROs are subordinate legislation and cannot modify the parent Act. If the owner has a ―lawful excuse‖ to be in possession of goods that are purportedly smuggled or prohibited or non-duty paid, no offence has been committed, and consequently the question of punishment or applicability of SROs issued under Section 181 does not come into play. Likewise, if the vehicle is not being used to ―remove‖ smuggled or proscribed goods, as explained earlier in this judgment, and the vehicle owner/operator is not found independently liable for an offence under Clause (89) or (90) of 45 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 Section 156(1) of the Act, such vehicle cannot be confiscated in terms of Section 157(2) of the Act.

56. Having established that the offences under Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Act require a mental element or culpability, we now turn to the scope of the impugned SROs. These notifications were issued under Section 181 of the Act. Let us delineate the nature and limits of this delegated power. The Supreme Court in Haji Tooti v. The Federal Board of Revenue (2023 SCMR 1980) analysed the interplay between Section 181 and Section 223 of the Customs Act. It noted that the power exercised by a customs officer under the main part of Section 181 (to give an option to pay fine in lieu of confiscation) is ―quasijudicial in nature‖. The Court distinguished the power under Section 181 from the administrative power under Section 223. It held that the provisos to Section 181, which authorize the FBR to specify goods or classes of goods where no option is to be given to pay redemption fine, or to fix the amount of fine, constitute delegated legislative power. While the Supreme Court accepted that the FBR can, through an SRO under Section 181, remove the discretion of the adjudicating officer to levy a fine and thereby mandate confiscation, it must be borne in mind that this power relates to the nature and quantum of punishment and becomes relevant after the constituent elements of the offence have been made out. In other words, the SROs only delineate the punishment or penalty for an already established offence.

57. This distinction is crucial for our purposes. Section 181 operates at the sentencing stage of the adjudicatory process. It determines the consequence of a finding of guilt. It does not empower the FBR to alter or dispense with the need to prove the 46 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 constituent elements of the offence itself, which are defined in Section 156. The definition of what constitutes an offence (the actus reus and mens rea) is a matter of substantive law, firmly rooted in the text of provisions of the Act. These provisions cannot be amended or altered by the issuance of an SRO under the limited power delegated by the Legislature to the FBR to determine the scope or nature of punishment to follow. Therefore, the reading of SRO 499 and SRO 1619 as transforming the offence of carrying smuggled goods into a ―strict liability offence‖ is flawed. The SROs, by their own terms, apply to ―lawfully registered conveyance... found carrying smuggled goods.‖ This presupposes that it has been determined that the goods in question are smuggled and that the person concerned was dealing with them ―without lawful excuse‖ as required by Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1). The SROs then apply in such scenario. The adjudicating officer cannot exercise discretion to substitute the punishment of confiscation with that of payment of redemption fine in lieu thereof. The principle of proportionality and its applicability to the penalty 58. Let us now examine the constitutionality and reasonableness of the mandatory confiscation prescribed by the SROs, particularly in light of the principle of proportionality. Even if the State has proven the elements of the offence, the penalty imposed must not be disproportionate to the gravity of the offence and the culpability of the offender.

59. The principle of proportionality is a well-recognized facet of substantive due process and is embedded in the constitutional guarantees of Pakistan. The Supreme Court in Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) v. ARY Communications (PLD 2023 SC 431) held that reasonable 47 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 restrictions on fundamental rights “must also proportionate in that the legitimate objective cannot reasonably be achieved through a means less restrictive of the right protected by the Constitution.” The concept of proportionality is embedded in the penal systems of other common law jurisdictions as well. In the United Kingdom, the Court of Appeal in R v. Bagnall [2012] EWCA Crim 677, while considering the fairness of a confiscation order, emphasized that the process must not lead to a result that is ―disproportionate‖ and must respect an individual's rights under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Court emphasized the need to ensure that the severity of the order matched the gravity of the offence, particularly where the consequences for the defendant were severe.

60. In the United States, the Eighth Amendment's prohibition against ―cruel and unusual punishments‖ has been interpreted to forbid punishments that are grossly disproportionate to the offence. The U.S. Supreme Court, in Solem v. Helm (463 U.S. 277, 1983), established a three-part test for proportionality, requiring courts to consider (i) the gravity of the offence and the harshness of the penalty, (ii) the sentences imposed on other criminals in the same jurisdiction, and (iii) the sentences imposed for the same crime in other jurisdictions. The Indian Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh ((1999) 6 SCC 172) observed that a mandatory sentence must not be ―arbitrary or oppressive‖ as that would violate Article 21 of the Indian Constitution and the right to life and liberty.

61. Proportionality is the standard that examines the relationship between a legitimate State objective and the means chosen to achieve it. The Supreme Court in PEMRA v. ARY 48 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 Communications held that a restriction that fetters a fundamental right must be the ―least restrictive means‖ to realize a legitimate objective. If the only possible reading of the SROs was that they mandate confiscation of the vehicle of an owner who is not culpable, but whose vehicle is incidentally found carrying smuggled, prohibited or non-duty paid goods, such punishment would fail the proportionality test.

62. Let us consider a scenario where a rental company or the bona fide owner of a truck rents it out to a third party. The third party, without the owner's knowledge or consent, loads it with smuggled goods. Under the interpretation advanced by the Customs Department, the truck is liable for mandatory confiscation. The owner, who is not culpable, would lose his asset. This would be manifestly unjust outcome. The principal offender (i.e. the person who smuggles goods or imports prohibited goods into the country) is the primary target of the Act. However, under the SROs, the punishment for an innocent vehicle owner (i.e. a bus owner carrying passengers possessing smuggled goods, or a transport vehicle owner providing carriage services) without knowledge or reasonable suspicion re the proscribed nature of goods being transported could face punishment that is identical to or greater than that faced by the principal offender. Such outcome violates the foundational principle that punishment should fit the crime and the degree of culpability. As noted earlier in this judgment, Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) allow for a ―lawful excuse‖. If the owner of a vehicle can prove that he is a bona fide purchaser for value without notice of the smuggled or proscribed nature of the goods he is transporting, or that he had no knowledge or any reasonable basis for suspicion that the goods 49 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 were smuggled, this would constitute a ―lawful excuse‖. To then mandate the confiscation of his/her property would render this statutory defence a nullity, violating both the letter and spirit of the Act.

63. There would be no limit to the absurd results that would flow from a contrary interpretation of the SROs read with Sections 156 and 157 of the Act. Could the Legislature have intended that a bus, train or airplane carrying or transporting smuggled or proscribed goods, while providing freight or transport services, be confiscated? Could the Legislature have designed Clause (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) as strict liability offences to confiscate rental vehicles being used to transport proscribed goods, with the vehicle owner or rental company possessing no means to control the actions of the renter? Could the Legislature have intended to impose the penalty of confiscation on a vehicle owner who, with no amount of diligence or exercise of duty of care, can prevent the commissioning of the proscribed act? Could the Legislature have intended to transform all courier and transport service providers into customs agents required to ensure that they never come in actual or constructive possession of goods that can be subsequently found to be smuggled or proscribed? What if you bought apples at a local fruit stall that were later found to be of Iranian origin and non-duty paid? Should your vehicle be confiscated for carrying smuggled/proscribed goods to your home?

64. The SROs, while valid as an exercise of the FBR's power under Section 181 to remove discretion in the imposition of a penalty, cannot be applied in a manner that ignores the principle of proportionality and the constitutional protections afforded to citizens. To apply them in a way that mandates confiscation 50 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 without any consideration of the owner's knowledge, consent, or bona fides would render the punishment arbitrary, excessive, and a breach of Article 10A (right to a fair trial and due process) read with Articles 9, 23 and 24 of the Constitution. While the FBR is vested with power under Section 181 to issue notifications like SRO 499 and SRO 1619, such notifications must be interpreted and applied in harmony with the provisions of the Act and the Constitution. The process of adjudication under the Act must first determine whether the essential elements of the offence under Clause (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) have been met, including the failure of the accused to establish a ―lawful excuse‖ for being in possession of smuggled or prohibited or non-duty paid goods. Once that determination is made and culpability for an offence is established, the SROs then operate to regulate the discretion available with adjudicatory authority in imposing the penalty.

65. For the reasons stated above we find as follows (and answer the questions framed for our consideration accordingly): (i) Mens rea is an essential ingredient of every offence unless some reason can be found for holding that that is not necessary, in order to give effect to the will of the Legislature as reflected from the words used in the text, when read in the context of the objects of the statute. It cannot be presumed that the Legislature intended to make an innocent individual liable for actions of persons over whom he/she has no control.

(ii) The objects of the Act do not include protection of public health, safety and morals or such other subject matter of social concern where it can be assumed that the Legislature intended imposition of strict liability to deter proscribed conduct. Neither will non-imposition of strict liability for offences in Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) defeat the objects of the Act, nor will its imposition augment the duty of care to be 51 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 exercised by an ordinary prudent person, which exercise will deter or curtail the incidence of such offences. The offences in Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Act are not strict liability offences and need establishment of mens rea as a precondition to hold a person liable for such offences. (iii) The imposition of the penalty of confiscation of a conveyance in terms of Section 157(2) of the Act in relation to the offences in Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Act requires prior establishment of the constituent elements of the offences, including the failure of the person concerned to prove a lawful excuse to be in possession of the smuggled/proscribed goods. And where a vehicle owner or operator is not directly charged with an offence under Clauses (89)

and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Act, his/her conveyance cannot be confiscated in terms of Section 157(2) of the Act, unless it is being employed, with his knowledge or wilful blindness to the suspicion, in ―removal‖ of smuggled or proscribed goods in an act proximate to the act of smuggling or importing/exporting proscribed goods, and not just for inland carrying or transport of such goods.

(iv) S.R.O. 499(I)/2009 and S.R.O. 1619(I)/2024, issued under Section 181 of the Customs Act, 1969, operate at the stage of sentencing. They do not, and cannot, alter or dispense with the requirement to prove the substantive elements of the offences prescribed in terms of Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Act.

(v) Where the Legislature has employed a broad set of verbs in a Clauses (89) and (90) of Section 156(1) of the Act but selects only a single, more restrictive verb for the confiscatory provision in Section 157(2), the principle of expressio unius est exclusio alterius dictates that the penalty is limited strictly to the act described. S.R.O. 499(I)/2009, S.R.O. 1619(I)/2024 or any other sub-statutory instrument issued in 52 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 exercise of authority under Section 181 of the Act, must operate within the four corners of the provisions of the Act and cannot expand, override or supplant such provisions. To the extent that the said SROs seek to expand the scope of confiscation of vehicles and conveyance beyond those employed to ―remove‖ proscribed goods, as provided in Section 157(2) of the Act, to those involved in ―carrying‖ or transporting proscribed goods, the SROs are ultra vires the Act, and are to be read down to that extent.

(vi) In applying these SROs, the Customs authorities, the Appellate Tribunal, and this Court must apply the principle of proportionality. Confiscation shall not be ordered where the owner of the conveyance found removing proscribed goods establishes lawful excuse for such removal, on a balance of probabilities, including, inter alia, that he/she was a bona fide owner with no knowledge or suspicion regarding the smuggled or proscribed nature of the goods, or that the conveyance was used for removal of proscribed goods without his/her consent or connivance and despite his/her exercise of reasonable diligence.

(vii) Once the offence in terms of Clauses (89) or (90) of Section 156(1) of the Act is made out as an evidentiary matter, and it has been determined on the basis of evidence/material on record that the conveyance was being used to ―remove‖ proscribed goods in terms of Section 157(2) of the Act, no adjudicatory authority is vested with discretion to impose redemption fine in lieu of confiscation of the vehicle in view of S.R.O. 499(I)/2009 and S.R.O.

1619(I)/2024. Once culpability of the defendant/s stands established, the adjudicatory authorities are left with no discretion for purposes of awarding penalty, and the confiscation of goods and/or vehicle, as the case may be, is mandatory.

(ix) Pending final adjudication, the Collector shall ordinarily exercise the discretion under the proviso to Section 157(2) of the Act to release a seized vehicle to its owner upon furnishing a sufficient financial guarantee, and any refusal to do so must be supported by recorded reasons.

110. As has been held and emphasized in some detail by this Court in Lal Mat Khan, where penal action has the effect of fettering fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, 77 | P a g e Cust. This principle is fully applicable during the adjudicatory process under provisions of the Act as well. In none of the twenty references that form the subject-matter before us have Collectors exercised their authority in terms of the first proviso to Section 157(2) of the Act, to release vehicles, subject to furnishing of financial guarantees, including where the vehicles-in-question were public transport carriers. In the event that the adjudicatory authorities come to the conclusion that the seized vehicle is not liable to confiscation, its seizure meanwhile denies its rightful owner the right to possession and use, which in turn also fetters the right guaranteed under Article 18 of the Constitution, to the extent that the vehicle is employed by the owner as part of his business. Such refusal to exercise the discretion vested in terms of the first proviso to Section 157(2) of the Act, becomes confiscatory where the no wrongdoing is found and the vehicle is ultimately ordered to be released. It is therefore imperative that the Collector ordinarily exercise such discretion to order the release of vehicles as a matter of course, subject to furnishing of guarantees. And the Collector must record reasons, where there exist grounds counselling against the exercise of such discretion, which grounds are then justiciable before the next appellate authority.

The consequences that flow from the adjudicatory orders are consequential for the interests of 78 | P a g e Cust. Ref. No.29/2025 citizens involved in the adjudicatory proceedings, as well as the interests of the state. There ought to be no need to emphasize that adjudicatory authorities are under an obligation to pass orders that are just, fair and reasonable, and are backed by proper reasoning, in terms of Section 24A of the General Clauses Act, 1897. Stereotypical, mechanical and cyclostyled orders or the cut-andpaste variety, without regard to the facts of individual cases, stand in clear breach of such duty.
